props.title: Cheyenne Autumn

sections.content: **Cheyenne Autumn** (1964) marks John Ford's final Western and his most direct attempt to address Hollywood's problematic portrayal of Native Americans. Unlike his earlier works like **The Searchers** (1956), Ford deliberately centers the Indigenous perspective, following the 1,500-mile journey of Northern Cheyenne trying to return to their ancestral lands. The film stands as a remarkable shift from typical 1960s Westerns, sharing thematic DNA with **Little Big Man** (1970) and **Soldier Blue** (1970) in challenging mainstream America's sanitized frontier mythology.

sections.content: Ford's visual mastery shines through even as he deconstructs his own Western legacy. The Monument Valley sequences echo his earlier works like **Stagecoach** (1939), but now these iconic landscapes serve as backdrop for Indigenous suffering rather than cowboy heroics. Richard Widmark's character, Captain Thomas Archer, represents the conflicted white conscience, similar to roles later explored in **Dances with Wolves** (1990).

The film's production context matters significantly. Shot during the height of the Civil Rights Movement, **Cheyenne Autumn** parallels contemporary struggles for racial justice. Ford cast Navajo actors to play Cheyenne roles (though still relied on some white actors in redface), while giving substantial screen time to Native perspectives - revolutionary for 1964 Hollywood. sections.content: While **Cheyenne Autumn** struggled at the box office, its influence resonates through later revisionist Westerns. Films like **Dead Man** (1995) and **Hostiles** (2017) build on its foundation of examining historical injustice through the Western genre. Even the controversial comedic interlude featuring James Stewart as Wyatt Earp (often cut from modern presentations) serves as meta-commentary on how Hollywood traditionally trivialized Native American experiences.
